system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-08-03 20:39:00 to 2175-08-06 17:21:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for confusion and reported bloody stools. His symptoms were attributed to hepatic encephalopathy, likely due to noncompliance with lactulose, with rapid improvement after restarting treatment. Evaluation for gastrointestinal bleeding showed no active bleed on guaiac testing or nasogastric lavage, and hematocrit remained stable. A preliminary blood culture showed coagulase-negative staph, but repeat cultures were negative, ruling out infection. He was discharged home with increased lactulose, addition of omeprazole, and adjustments to other medications, including reduced fluoxetine and tamoxifen doses. He was alert, oriented, and hemodynamically stable at discharge.
problems: Chronic hepatitis C with hepatic coma
Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol

radiology_notes.text:
EXAM:  MRI of the lumbar spine.

CLINICAL INFORMATION:  Patient with history of lumbar stenosis and back pain,
worsening for the last two weeks associated with urinary incontinence and
weakness.  Rule out cauda equina syndrome.

TECHNIQUE:  T1 and T2 sagittal and T2 axial images of the lumbar spine were
obtained.

FINDINGS:  At T11-12 to L1-2, no abnormalities are seen.  At L2-3, L4-5
degenerative disc disease and minimal bulging seen.  At L3-4 and L4-5,
widening of the facet joints are seen secondary to degenerative change.  No
spinal stenosis or foraminal narrowing noted at these levels.

At L5-S1 level, the endplates demonstrate low T1 signal with slight increased
T2 signal indicative of endplate degenerative change.  In absence of
surrounding soft tissue changes or epidural changes of the appearances of the
endplates more likely to be degenerative change.  There is a small central
protrusion seen which extends slightly to the right of midline.  However,
there is no displacement of the nerve roots or compression of the thecal sac
seen.  There is moderate left-sided and mild right-sided foraminal narrowing
at L5-S1 level.

The distal spinal cord shows normal signal intensities.

IMPRESSION:  Degenerative endplate disease and disc degenerative change at
L5-S1 level with moderate left foraminal and mild right foraminal narrowing
and small central disc protrusion.  No compression of the thecal sac or
displacement of nerve roots seen.  No evidence of cauda equina compression. 
Degenerative changes at other levels as described above.

HISTORY:  End-stage liver disease, with back pain, evaluate for any pockets of
ascites, and if present, please mark spot for paracentesis.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  Targeted grayscale evaluation was performed over the four quadrants
of the abdomen.  No ascites is identified.  Partially imaged is an enlarged
spleen measuring up to 19.2 cm and probable varices in the epigastrium.

IMPRESSION:  No ascites identified.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand you've been having a lot of back pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been getting worse over the past two weeks. Last week it really flared up. It’s in the middle of my back and goes down both sides, worse on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. But I did fall today because I felt unsteady. The pain makes it hard to move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you mentioned some urine leakage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, just a little when I delay going to the bathroom because of the pain. Never a big accident or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. No saddle numbness or bowel issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy before. Have you been taking your lactulose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, I’ve skipped it for about a week. It’s hard to get up to go to the bathroom with this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable, but we need to keep your bowels moving to avoid confusion. We’ll help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had an MRI in the ER. It showed degenerative disc disease at L5-S1, with some narrowing and a small disc bulge. But no nerve compression or cauda equina.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s pinched? Is that good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s good. It means no emergency surgery. But the degeneration and muscle spasms are causing significant pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been asking for Valium. It helps the spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you diazepam for spasms, but carefully. Because of your liver disease, sedatives can build up and cause confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get confused easily if I take too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’ll use it only as needed, and stop if you feel drowsy or confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad, especially when I move. Can I get more Valium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can have another dose. We’re also starting tizanidine, another muscle relaxant. But same rule—stop if you feel sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the oxycodone helps, but I worry about constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ahead of that. We’ve added senna and docusate to keep your bowels moving. And we’ve increased your lactulose to four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I don’t want another episode of confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re monitoring your mental status closely. You’re still clear, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound to check for ascites, since you mentioned some weight gain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No ascites found. But we did see an enlarged spleen and some varices, which we already knew about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing urgent. Your liver condition is stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain improving at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little. The meds help, but I still can’t walk far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged outpatient physical therapy. They’ll teach you safe movements and exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be good. I don’t want to be on these painkillers forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on the same page. We’re also giving you a lidocaine patch for the back. Apply it for 12 hours, then remove for 12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll follow up with your liver doctor and now also with the chronic pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue oxycodone as needed, diazepam and tizanidine for spasms, but stop them as pain improves. And crucially—do not take Ambien while on diazepam or tizanidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember. And keep up the lactulose and rifaximin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And the stool softeners. If you feel confused, stop all new meds and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep that follow-up appointment.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with worsening low back pain and muscle spasms over two weeks, complicated by difficulty moving due to pain and recent noncompliance with lactulose. MRI showed degenerative disc disease at L5-S1 without nerve compression or cauda equina. Pain was managed with oxycodone, diazepam, tizanidine, and a lidocaine patch. Due to his history of hepatic encephalopathy, bowel regimen was intensified with lactulose, senna, and docusate to prevent constipation. He remained mentally clear throughout. No ascites was found on ultrasound. He was discharged home with a plan for outpatient physical therapy, follow-up in the chronic pain clinic, and clear instructions to avoid sedating medications if confusion develops.
